There are about 30 satellites and they orbit the Earth at a distance of around 20,000 km.  Each satellite has a signal that can be picked up by a receiver.  A GPS receiver can use this signal to calculate its position and orientation, and to estimate the clocks of the receiver and the satellites.  Most GPS devices have an accuracy of around 10 meters.

The signal from one of the satellites is modulated (uploaded) to a lower frequency signal that can be received by other GPS devices.  This allows other GPS devices to receive the signal from the higher orbiting satellite and calculate their own positions.  A GPS receiver will also include a receiver that can measure the Doppler effect of the received signal.  This can give an estimate of the satellite’s position and speed and allow the receiver to know if the clock of the receiver is correct.  All this information can then be processed by the GPS receiver to calculate its own position.

It’s useful to think of a GPS receiver as a radio receiver in human-sized form.  The radio signal is modulated and transmitted from the satellites, which is much more efficient than sending and receiving the signal directly.  Instead of picking up the radio signal, the GPS receiver looks for a signal that has been modulated to a lower frequency.  This allows the GPS receiver to “hop” over to the next satellite and receive the data from that satellite.  The GPS receiver can then store some of this information and make a prediction of its own position based on this information and a guess about the speed of the satellite.
